newsitem.title: INDIA: No sign yet of India industry revival - ING Barings.
newsitem.headline: No sign yet of India industry revival - ING Barings.

text.p: There is very little evidence to indicate that a recent industrial slowdown of the Indian economy has been capped and that the worst is over, securities firm ING Barings said on Tuesday.
"It would seem that people are now wishing that the worst is over; there is very little cogent evidence to prove the revival theory," ING Barings said in its February report on India.
Industrial growth slowed to 9.8 percent in April-September 1996 compared with 12.1 percent a year earlier but some analysts have forecast a turnaround, beginning in the last quarter of 1996.
ING Barings said it disagreed with the consensus view that a bumper agricultural production was likely to propel industrial revival and economic growth in 1997.
"An analysis of economic data over the last 20 years shows no correlation whatsoever between agricultural and industrial growth, with or without lag effects," the report said.

It said quality and reliability of agricultural data was historically poor and added that growing consumerism in rural India should not be construed to be a function of increasing annual disposable income in the hands of farmers.

"Although agriculture supports 70 percent of the population, its contribution to GDP is only 30 percent, indicating that large sections of the agrarian population are not part of the market economy which drives industrial growth," it said.
ING Barings said another popular myth was that increased liquidity would drive industrial growth.
"Poor bank advances are a symptom and not a cause of the continuing industrial slowdown," the report said, pointing out that banks had been complaining that credit sanctions were under-utilised.
Falling real interest rates were also unlikely to impact short-term production targets, which are primarily driven by demand for immediate consumption, the securities firm said.

It said recent policy changes to boost investments in the core sector would lead to economic growth in the long run but actual inflows in the next two years were unlikely to be spectacular enough to trigger economic growth in that period.
But ING Barings saw some light at the end of the tunnel.
"We believe that the deep industrial slowdown and evaporating corporate earnings being witness currently carry within them the seeds of burgeoning growth," it said.
It said creaking infrastructure, a stagnating economy and bloated fiscal deficits of the state and federal government would force the government to take action.

"Due to the limited options available, a political consensus will be arrived at and major structural reforms will be implemented to restore fiscal discipline and woo foreign investment in earnest," ING Barings said.
